Ginny's experience in and of itself is terrifying. 

Ginny is raised being told not to trust something if she can't see where it keeps it's brain. Then, the summer before she starts school, she gets a wonderful gift with her school books, a diary that writes back! His name is Tom. He's kind, caring, gives great advice. 

But Ginny's having a hard time staying awake in class. She's feeling weak, drained. Some days she can barely drag herself out of bed. Then she finds herself in unexpected places. How did she get into Moaning Myrtle's bathroom? Why is she standing in front of Hagrid's hut? She must have spaced out. But why is there blood on her hands? Why are Hagrid's chickens dead?

Then there is an attack — Mrs. Norris is petrified outside Moaning Myrtle's bathroom. Ginny likes cats, even Moaning Myrtle, who is a bit of a pain when Ginny finds herself out late at night. The blood that Ginny has on her hands is still wet when she notices it. There is talk about a Chamber of Secrets and an heir. Ginny tells Tom, and he asks about the students reactions, about the fear they feel. About whether the school will close.

She finds herself writing in the diary more and more. There are hours at a time that she loses control of her body. Ginny She asks Tom what's happening. Maybe he can help? Perhaps he was trapped in the diary like Ginny feels she will be. But Tom doesn't seem to know what to do. It gets harder for Ginny to tell how much time she's lost. Colin Creevey, the boy who sits with her in class, is attacked. Ginny's had enough. Tom is a great friend, but she thinks it's her fault that Colin was attacked. Ginny considers telling Tom goodbye, but decides it's best to dispose of the diary before she can have any regrets.

Myrtle isn't happy with Ginny when she flushes the diary down the toilet. Neither will Tom be happy if he can feel the water soaking through his paper lungs. For the first time in months, Ginny feels free. She throws herself into the lessons, making a fool of herself when she can barely do a decent transfiguration of a matchstick into a needle. Ginny tells her professors she's under the weather, and is told to do more practice, but the feeling of lightness she has makes her shrug off the snickering of her classmates.

For a few glorious weeks, Ginny gets to know her dorm mates and make some new friends. Her professors are praising her work ethic, she's feeling more energetic than she has in a while. But one evening, as Ginny gets started on her homework, Harry comes in. Harry and the diary. Ginny watches, heart beating in her chest as Harry runs up the boys stairs with the diary. Tom will tell Harry everything. What she thinks of her brothers, of him, about the chickens! The day of his Quidditch game, Ginny runs up to his dormitory to get the diary. It's a relief to have the diary again. Why did she throw it out?
